I have no light. That means: I do not belong to the world of German Idealism.
Delight in Cardinal Melchior de Polignac’s Anti-Lucretius, printed in 1754.
In the preface there is already the couplet that supplied the feathers with which Franklin was later adorned, and which glorifies Epicurus:
“Assailing the thunderous temples of heaven, he snatched the thunderbolt from Jove and the arrows from Phoebus.”
In Books II and III there are delightful hexameters about atoms and infinity.
Especially beautiful are these lines on eternal recurrence, pp. 95–96:
“Nor does it help to imagine countless worlds elsewhere, where an unlimited abundance of every kind of thing bursts forth without measure, while our own world receives so little …
Atoms must have a measure, a limit, and a bridle.”
I want to send that last line to Heisenberg or Pascual Jordan.
I walk around this landscape of the Lenne valley.
If landscape is an état d’âme, a state of the soul, then I am apparently walking around inside myself.

Inside the memories of my youth, and so on. This is obviously even more dangerous than having conversations with oneself. It is an occasio proxima, a near occasion, for every sin of subjectivism, egotism, and armoring the self. It is a self-created paradise in which I play both the part of God the Creator and the part of Adam.
The cultivated person walks through a landscape carrying quotations from poets and philosophers, memories of classical or Romantic paintings, Impressionist or Expressionist paintings.
In short: he walks through the landscape as though he were walking through a library and an art gallery. He enjoys his education. That means: he enjoys his own enlarged self.
Surely belief in law is really belief in the lawgiver.
In Michelet’s Pologne et Russie of 1852 this belief is almost touching.
Humanity no longer has a father as the source of authority.
Law has taken the father’s place.
That is why the crisis of legality is more than just another temporary difficulty.
According to Michelet, the geographical boundary of this new faith is: the Vistula!
Deeply moved by Kütemeyer’s afterword to Kierkegaard’s The Concept of Irony. He writes in the same annihilatingly polemical tone as Theodor Haecker.
And in Haecker’s own style he destroys poor Theodor Haecker because Haecker quoted one of Kierkegaard’s pseudonyms as though it were Kierkegaard himself.
The truly rabid ones fighting among themselves.
Poor Haecker has already been overtaken by his.
Today his Satire and Polemic of 1926/27 has to be carefully kept quiet by his admirers.
Haecker’s false reputation has been grafted onto this wild shoot.
Wilhelm, the destroyer of the destroyer? And his own transformation?
The completely solitary man as holder of License No. 32.
He will not escape his fate.
Judge not, that you be not judged.
“from printer’s ink scattered by the wind.” Now it comes back to confront me. Now it is thrown into my eyes.
But again and again: hide your life and spread your spirit.
Annette writes to Sprickmann, Cardauns, Letters, p. 9:
Your dear image “always remains a pure, quiet ground on which I can paint whatever I wish.”
Klemens M.[öllenbrock], p. 70, quotes this as an example of how the object is transformed into an occasio, an occasion. But Annette says ground. How profound that word is in her. And how un-Romantic.
Deeply frightened by the real irony contained in the fact that a thick book about the concept of irony is lying in my room.
Irony is so actively destructive that merely naming it determines the whole atmosphere.
Perhaps the same is true of every concept and every word. That is conceptual realism.
To be the victim of the irony of world history, the irony of fate—that is unbearable.
Unbearable even as a hypothetical possibility.
Even as a danger or a risk.
God is easy to deceive. But God cannot deceive.
In fact, that is almost what it always is.
Were you deception, you blessed silver-blue day? Or, worse still: were you irony?
Because when the strong practice irony upon the weak, irony becomes the most terrible form of cruelty.
There is something almost animal-like in the matter-of-fact way Hegel knows himself to be identical with the subject of the “irony of history.” He shows no fear when speaking of such things.
So does Hegel too belong to that little nation of people who never sense the Devil?
Descartes’ deepest motive, the final thing driving him, was fear of the spiritus malignus: fear of the abyss contained in the possibility of ironic deception.
I have a sin to confess.
At the end of August 1946, in the despair of the camp, early one morning as the first rays of sunlight fell across my bunk, I spoke aloud to the sun and said:
Like the statement Kierkegaard’s father once made about God.
Since then my external circumstances have improved, and the worst mistreatment has stopped.
Is all of this, then, deception?
A desperate entanglement in the labyrinth of negations.
The deadly rebound of this ugly stone once one has thrown it.
What remains once a person has allowed himself to enter the realm of irony?
I stand there like a ghost and scream without a throat. And yet I myself made practical use of the most intense irony.
The ironic superiority of the person who knows over Papageno or Caliban.
Expecting far too much hidden goodness from them.
In doing this I committed an injustice for which Kierkegaard too felt guilty:
I placed Caliban in a test that was bound to drive him deeper into wickedness as soon as he sensed my irony.
My irony inflamed his hatred. And he attributed that irony to the cause he believed I represented:
Stirner’s irrefutability lies in the fact that a single empirical I knows how to use the weapon of irony consistently.
In an age built around the philosophy of the I, this I stands beyond every attack.
Ego cogito, ergo ego sum. I think, therefore I am.
Sum, sum, sum—little bee, buzz around.
The infinite ambiguity of the word “I” gives it an infinite number of ironic hiding places and possibilities for attack.
I alone. And therefore I define, interpret, and illustrate Myself and tolerate no intervention from forces foreign to the I.
At one moment I am the intelligible I.
